paper_sections.title: Multiple brain networks contribute to the acquisition of bias in perceptual decision-making
The neural correlates of the acquired bias in perceptual decisions
Learning signals for the acquisition of bias in perceptual decisions
The changes in functional connectivity as the bias grows

description.value: The study examined how reward-context information is learned and integrated with sensory evidence to produce bias in motion discrimination decisions, and identified the neural correlates and functional connectivity changes associated with this acquired bias.

design.value: Participants performed a motion discrimination task during fMRI acquisition. Pre-trial contextual cues signaled one of two reward contexts, and trial-wise reward feedback reinforced one of the two motion-direction choices more strongly in each context. Behavioral choices were modeled with hierarchical logistic regression and reinforcement-learning models, and fMRI data were analyzed with parametric GLMs and PPI analyses.

description.value: Twenty-four human participants completed the behavioral paradigm in the MRI scanner; one participant was excluded because of extreme parameter estimates in the fMRI data analysis. The group analyses therefore included 23 participants.

inclusion_criteria.value: Free of any self-reported neurological or psychiatric diseases

exclusion_criteria.value: Extreme parameter estimates, with orders of magnitude different from the other subjects, in the fMRI data analysis

recruitment_method.value: Recruited through posted flyers and prescreened

medical_condition.value: No self-reported neurological or psychiatric diseases

task_description.value: Participants first performed a practice session in the laboratory to familiarize themselves with the random-dot motion discrimination task. A trial began with a red fixation cross for 1.5 s, followed by a 200-ms moving-dot patch; participants decided whether the global motion direction was upward or downward by pressing the corresponding spatially congruent buttons within 600 ms.

presentation_software.value: Matlab version 7.10.0, using the Psychophysics Toolbox extension, version 3.0.10

instructions.value: Participants had to decide whether the global motion direction of the dots was upward or downward by pressing the corresponding spatially congruent buttons.

stimuli.value: Each motion stimulus was composed of 150 white dots moving inside a donut-shaped display patch on a black background. The display patch extended from 4 to 8 degrees of visual angle, dots moved at 8 degrees of visual angle per second, and each stimulus comprised 12 video frames with a 60-Hz refresh rate.

task_performance_measures.value: Choice of upward or downward motion direction

task_name.value: motion discrimination task with reward contexts

task_description.value: During fMRI acquisition, participants decided the motion direction of moving dots in two independent reward contexts with the goal of obtaining as many reward points as possible. A colored fixation cross signaled the context, a 200-ms motion stimulus was presented, participants had up to 800 ms from stimulus onset to respond, and reward feedback was then presented for 1.5 s.

design_type.value: event-related task with jittered inter-trial intervals

presentation_software.value: Matlab version 7.10.0, using the Psychophysics Toolbox extension, version 3.0.10

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to decide the motion direction on each trial in order to harvest the most reward points.

stimuli.value: A patch of moving dots was presented after a blue or yellow fixation cross. The motion stimulus was randomly sampled from seven coherence levels: 0, ±4, ±12, and ±64%.

description.value: Functional data were collected using a T2-weighted multi-band echo-planar imaging sequence with a 60-degree flip angle. Forty-eight oblique axial slices were collected in interleaved fashion. The slices were tilted at a 10–15-degree angle off the anterior-commissure-posterior-commissure line, and higher-order shimming was applied to reduce dropout in orbitofrontal cortex.
T1-weighted anatomical images were collected using an MP-RAGE sequence with a 9-degree flip angle, 256-mm field of view, 256 × 256 matrix, 192 slices, and 1-mm slice thickness.

fMRI data preprocessing was carried out using FSL Version 5.0.1. Image time series were aligned, motion-related measures and bad time points were identified, images were skull stripped, spatially smoothed, grand-mean intensity normalized, high-pass filtered, and registered to structural and standard-space images.

steps.value: Align all image time series with the MCFLIRT tool
Use motion parameters to compute frame-wise displacement and DVARS and identify bad time points using FD > 0.5 and DVARS > 0.5
Skull stripping of functional images with BET and structural images with FreeSurfer
Spatial smoothing with a Gaussian kernel of 5-mm FWHM
Grand-mean intensity normalization over the entire 4D dataset by a single multiplicative factor
High-pass temporal filtering using Gaussian-weighted least-squares straight-line fitting with sigma = 50.0 s
Apply the same high-pass filter to the fMRI design matrix
Register functional images to the high-resolution structural image using Boundary-Based Registration
Register the high-resolution structural image to the MNI-152 2-mm template using FLIRT linear registration with 12 degrees of freedom
Include motion correction parameters, FD, DVARS, and single-time-point regressors for time points exceeding the FD/DVARS thresholds to perform scrubbing

model_settings.value: The full model included coherence-level, reward context, run-number, context-by-run, and coherence-by-run interaction regressors. The intercept was treated as a random effect across participants. Chi-square tests compared the full model with reduced models.

estimator.value: Chi-square test comparing goodness-of-fit of full and reduced models

model_type.value: context-dependent Q-learning reinforcement-learning model with a logit choice function

model_settings.value: Choice probability was modeled from the subjective value difference between upward and downward motion and the coherence level. Context-dependent reward prediction errors updated the value of the chosen motion direction in the specific context. Free parameters included the choice sensitivity to value difference and motion stimulus and the context-dependent learning rate. Initial action values were initialized from participants' initial bias in the practice session when present.

estimator.value: maximum likelihood; free parameters were fit by minimizing the negative log likelihood with a non-linear optimization function

software.value: Scipy toolbox for Python, fmin optimization function

model_type.value: context-free Q-learning reinforcement-learning model with a logit choice function

model_settings.value: Choice probability was modeled from the subjective value difference between upward and downward motion and the coherence level. The context-free reward prediction error updated the value of each motion direction regardless of context. Free parameters included the choice sensitivity to value difference and motion stimulus and the context-free learning rate.

estimator.value: maximum likelihood; free parameters were fit by minimizing the negative log likelihood with a non-linear optimization function

software.value: Scipy toolbox for Python, fmin optimization function

hrf_model.value: double-gamma hemodynamic response function with temporal derivatives

model_settings.value: The first-level model was estimated separately for each run and participant. Five runs were combined within participant using a fixed-effects model, and FLAME 1 mixed-effects modeling was applied at the group level. Parametric regressors modeled absolute coherence, trial-wise amount of bias, and context-based and context-free reward prediction errors. Nuisance regressors modeled trial-evoked activity, reaction time, and motion-related confounds. All values of parametric regressors were mean-centered. Statistical maps were corrected with cluster-based random field theory using clusters determined by Z > 2.3 and a family-wise-error-corrected cluster significance threshold of P = 0.05.

level.value: first-level, within-participant fixed-effects, and group-level mixed-effects

estimator.value: FSL FEAT first-level GLM, fixed-effects combination across runs, and FLAME 1 mixed-effects group model

model_settings.value: Three independent PPI analyses used 10-mm spherical seed regions centered on vmPFC at MNI [−6, 39, −8], left frontal cortex at [−45, 21, 0], and left parietal cortex at [−36, −39, 45]. The PPI interaction between the seed signal and trial-wise amount of bias was generated in the neural domain, reconvolved, and added to the GLM with the raw seed time course.

level.value: first-level for each participant and run

estimator.value: PPI regression using the above-mentioned GLM design matrix with raw seed time course and PPI regressors

At the beginning of a trial, the fixation-cross color changed to yellow for 1 s to signal the other reward context. The association between color and payoff was counter-balanced across participants.

definition.value: Activation positively correlates with the amount of acquired bias from trial to trial.

multiple_comparison_method.value: cluster-based random field theory with family-wise error correction

interpretations.value: The amount of bias in perceptual decisions can be modeled as the subjective value difference between the two motion directions.
